parts.partTitle: Static Nested Classes vs. Memory-Leaking Inner Classes

beats.headline: Is your background task keeping 50 megabytes pinned in memory?
beats.subline: A non-static inner class silently holds a synthetic reference to its outer instance.
beats.narration: Dropping a class reference won't save you from an OutOfMemoryError if an inner class stays alive. A non-static inner class silently holds a hidden synthetic pointer to its enclosing object.

beats.title: Inner Class Heap Pointer Trap
beats.subtitle: How non-static inner classes prevent garbage collection

nodes.label: OrderBatchProcessor
nodes.detail: Holds 50MB byte array working buffer in heap memory

nodes.label: CompletionNotifier
nodes.detail: Non-static inner Runnable with synthetic this$0 pointer

nodes.label: Scheduled Executor Queue
nodes.detail: Holds active reference to Runnable until delay expires

nodes.label: Garbage Collector
nodes.detail: Cannot reclaim 50MB outer buffer due to reachable path

beats.narration: When a inner class is declared without static, javac injects a synthetic field named this dollar zero. If that inner task sits in an executor queue, the entire 50 megabyte outer allocation stays pinned.

beats.title: Fixing the Retention Bug with Static

steps.explanation: Decouples inner class from outer heap instance—no synthetic this$0 reference is created.
Pass only the exact scalar fields needed into constructor instead of capturing whole object.

beats.narration: Declare nested classes static whenever they do not explicitly require instance fields of the outer class. Pass only the scalar data needed into the constructor to break the hidden heap chain.

beats.title: Disassembling Synthetic Fields with javap
beats.caption: Inspecting the hidden compiler-generated field

lines.text: # Inspect internal fields of non-static inner class
final BankAccount this$0; // Synthesized outer reference!

beats.narration: Running javap on a non-static inner class file reveals the truth. The compiler generates a synthetic final field named this dollar zero and passes the outer instance straight into the constructor.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Static nested classes have zero outer instance overhead
Non-static inner classes keep outer instances alive via this$0
Default to static nested classes per Effective Java Item 24

parts.partTitle: Local Classes, Anonymous Types & Stack Captures

beats.headline: Why does Java fail to compile if you reassign a captured variable?
beats.subline: Stack frames vanish on return, but heap objects outlive method calls.
beats.narration: Try reassigning a variable right before passing it to a lambda or anonymous class, and javac throws a red compile error. The reason lies in how the Java memory stack differs from the heap.

beats.title: Stack Lifetime vs. Heap Lifetime

top.label: Stack Frame (Method Scope)
points: Stack frame disappears as soon as method returns
Reassignment causes stack and heap values to drift

bottom.label: Captured Heap Field
points: Compiler copies value into synthetic heap field
Effectively final rule keeps copies in perfect sync

beats.narration: Stack variables vanish when a method returns, but an anonymous Runnable resides on the heap and runs later. Java copies the value into a hidden field on the object, so mutation is forbidden to prevent copies from drifting.

beats.title: Anonymous Class vs. Lambda Scope

steps.explanation: Creates a distinct runtime object that can hold its own instance fields and state.
Inside an anonymous class, 'this' points to the inner instance, NOT the outer class scope.

beats.narration: Unlike lambdas where this refers to the enclosing class, inside an anonymous inner class this refers to the anonymous instance itself. Anonymous classes can also hold mutable fields and implement multi-method interfaces.

beats.title: Compiler Error on Variable Reassignment
beats.caption: Demonstrating the effectively final check

lines.text: AuditTask.java:12: error: local variables referenced from an
inner class must be final or effectively final
# Fix: remove reassignment or create a dedicated local copy

beats.narration: If you reassign a captured local variable anywhere in the enclosing method, javac halts compilation instantly. The variable must be assigned exactly once to qualify as effectively final.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Local capture copies stack variables to synthetic heap fields
Captured variables must be final or effectively final
Inside anonymous classes, 'this' refers to the inner instance

parts.partTitle: Java 16 Records & The Shallow Immutability Trap

beats.headline: Java records are not as immutable as you think.
beats.subline: Record fields are private final references, but referenced collections stay mutable.
beats.narration: Declaring a Java record generates private final fields, but if one component is an ArrayList or array, callers can still mutate your internal state. Here is how shallow immutability traps production apps.

beats.title: Shallow vs. Deep Immutability

top.label: Naive Record Declaration
points: List reference is final, but list content is mutable
Callers can modify internal state directly

bottom.label: Compact Constructor Copy
points: Mutating caller list no longer affects record

beats.narration: Notice the vulnerability in naive records. The items component reference is final, but the underlying list can still be mutated. Using a compact constructor with List dot copyOf guarantees true immutability.

beats.title: Compact Constructors & Validation

steps.explanation: No parameter signature needed—runs validation before direct field assignment.
Reassigns local parameter to immutable copy before final compiler assignment.

beats.narration: Compact constructors let you validate rules and perform defensive copies without re-declaring field assignments. The parameter reassignments run seamlessly right before the compiler sets final record fields.

beats.caption: Confirming Record inheritance and generated methods

beats.narration: Inspecting class files reveals records automatically extend java lang Record. Notice generated accessors use component names directly like orderId without traditional get prefixes.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Records are shallowly immutable by default
Use compact constructors for validation and defensive copies
Records automatically extend java.lang.Record and generate canonical constructors

beats.headline: Traditional Java serialization bypasses constructors, but records fix it.
beats.subline: Record deserialization forces data through canonical validation constructors.
beats.narration: Standard Java Object Serialization bypasses constructors entirely and injects raw byte streams directly into private fields. Records fix this major security flaw by routing deserialization straight through your canonical constructor.

beats.title: Safe Serialization Pipeline
beats.subtitle: How records guarantee validation invariants on deserialization

nodes.label: Incoming Byte Stream
nodes.detail: Serialized record components payload from external source

nodes.label: Canonical Constructor
nodes.detail: JVM invokes record constructor with stream values

nodes.label: Compact Validation
nodes.detail: Compact constructor checks non-null & non-negative invariants

nodes.label: Validated Record Instance
nodes.detail: Guaranteed valid memory state or throws InvalidObjectException

beats.narration: Traditional deserialization constructs objects without calling constructors, bypassing safety checks. For records, Java deserialization extracts component values and passes them to the canonical constructor, enforcing compact constructor validations.

beats.title: Java 21 Record Patterns (JEP 440)

steps.explanation: Deconstructs outer Account and nested Money record directly into local variables.
Variables owner, amt, and curr are bound and ready for immediate type-safe use.

beats.narration: In Java 21, pattern matching allows deconstructing nested records inside instanceof and switch expressions. Components like owner, amount, and currency extract cleanly without tedious getter calls.

beats.title: Records vs. JPA Entities

top.label: JPA / Hibernate Entity
points: Requires no-arg constructor and mutable fields for proxies

bottom.label: Immutable DTO / Value Object
points: Perfect for API requests, responses, and Map keys
Compiler provides equals, hashCode, and accessors

beats.narration: Records make ideal data transfer objects and key types. However, do not use records as JPA entities, because ORM frameworks require mutable fields, lazy proxies, and no-argument constructors.
